title: Integrated photovoltaics need design innovation and cross-sector collaboration - Nature Energy
text:
The wish to produce sustainable solar energy everywhere, reduce dependence on the grid as well as enable innovative design is stimulating the development of integrated photovoltaic (IPV) applications. IPV refers to solar-power-generating PV components that are inherently integrated into the design of objects, including products, structures, buildings, and automotive parts, instead of being simply added or retrofitted on top of the existing surfaces of conventional products1. Unlike conventional PV systems, where design and aesthetics are secondary to energy production, IPV transforms PV technology into a product-integrated and functionally integrated design feature.IPV applications have existed for decades, but their future success depends on rethinking how PV technologies are designed and developed. Conventional PV innovation has primarily focused on increasing efficiency and reducing cost, whereas IPV requires PV technologies to become integrated design elements of products, vehicles and buildings. In addition to energy generation, IPV must therefore address product-specific requirements, including aesthetics, form factor, functionality and user experience. Achieving this transition will require not only advances in PV technology but also closer collaboration between the PV sector and other industries.
